summary: Provides example TLS 1.3 handshakes, with private keys and inputs so they can be reproduced. Intermediate values such as secrets, traffic keys and IVs are shown so implementers can check their code step by step.

eli5.summary: A math book shows worked answers so you can check your own. This shows a full worked TLS 1.3 handshake so programmers can see if theirs matches.

subtitle: Worked examples for testing TLS 1.3 implementations

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 adds complex cryptographic operations with many derived secrets. Implementers need test vectors to verify each step of their handshakes works correctly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8448 provides complete example TLS 1.3 handshakes with all private keys, public keys, inputs, and intermediate values exposed, allowing implementations to check their outputs incrementally.
tldr.outcome: Developers can compare their implementation outputs against the examples to find bugs early, without needing working TLS 1.3 implementations at both ends.

facts.label: Number of examples
facts.value: 5 (simple 1-RTT, resumed 0-RTT, HelloRetryRequest, client authentication, compatibility mode)

facts.label: Handshake flow
facts.value: ClientHello, ServerHello, EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished

today: RFC 8448 remains the primary source of TLS 1.3 test vectors and is widely used by implementations to verify their handshake processing. The examples have become the de facto standard for checking TLS 1.3 implementation correctness.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 defines a new key schedule and cryptographic operations that are more complex than earlier versions. This RFC provides sample handshakes with all intermediate values visible: the private keys, public keys, salts, and every derived secret and traffic key. Each cryptographic step is labeled so an implementation can verify outputs independently.

A private key is included so implementations can reproduce the handshakes exactly. The traces show the output of every HKDF operation, every hash, and every encryption step. This allows an implementation to find bugs in its key derivation, hashing, or encryption without needing a working peer to test against.
sections.eli5: When you build a secure connection, you do a lot of secret math. This shows all the answers so you can check if you did it right.

sections.title: Example Handshakes Provided
sections.content:
RFC 8448 includes five worked handshake examples. The first is the simplest 1-RTT handshake, where the server is authenticated and the client remains anonymous. The client sends a ClientHello, the server responds with ServerHello, then exchanges EncryptedExtensions and Certificate messages, followed by CertificateVerify and Finished messages to complete the handshake with authentication.

Later examples show more complex scenarios: a resumed session with 0-RTT data, a HelloRetryRequest when key agreement needs renegotiation, client authentication with a CertificateVerify from the client, and a compatibility mode that makes TLS 1.3 appear as TLS 1.2 to middleboxes. Each example includes the complete byte-for-byte output of every message and all intermediate cryptographic values.
sections.eli5: Different kinds of secure conversations happen: first-time connections, reconnections, and connections where both sides prove who they are. This shows examples of all of them, with all the secret numbers used.

sections.title: Key Schedule and Secrets
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 uses HKDF (HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function) to derive all secrets from the initial secret material. The process starts with an early secret derived from a zero salt and zero-filled bytes, then uses HKDF to expand it. After the client and server exchange ephemeral keys, a handshake secret is extracted. From the handshake secret, client and server traffic keys are derived, used only during the handshake phase. Finally, a master secret is extracted and used to derive application data traffic keys.

Each derived value shown in the traces (such as traffic key and initialization vector) follows this schedule. The RFC shows the PRK (pseudorandom key) after extract, the hash input, and the expanded key output for every derivation step. Implementing the key schedule correctly is critical because a single bit error in a secret will cause all subsequent traffic keys to be wrong.
sections.eli5: Making secure keys is like a recipe with lots of steps. You start with some secret, run it through a blender, take the result and run it through another step, and so on until you have the final key for talking. This shows every step of that recipe.

sections.title: Cryptographic Primitives
sections.content:
The examples use specific cryptographic algorithms: x25519 for ephemeral key exchange, SHA-256 for hashing, AES-128-GCM for encryption, and ECDSA with SHA-256 for signatures. Each example shows the byte-level output of these operations. For instance, the ServerHello is encrypted under a derived handshake traffic key and results in a record with specific bytes. The CertificateVerify message contains a signature over the handshake hash, computed by hashing all prior handshake messages.

The traces allow implementers to test each primitive independently. An implementation can check that its SHA-256 produces the same hash values, that its HKDF produces the same derived keys, that its AES-GCM produces the same ciphertexts, and that its ECDSA signature verification works correctly on the provided signature bytes. This incremental checking is more useful than trying to get a complete handshake working at once.
sections.eli5: You use special math (x25519, SHA-256, AES) to do the secrets. This shows what answer you should get for each piece of math, so you can check if you coded it right.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These test vectors are provided solely for implementation verification and MUST NOT be used for deployment. The private keys and intermediate values are all public, so any implementation using them would be trivially broken. Real deployments must use fresh keys and secrets generated cryptographically.

These examples show the correct output format and values for the most common TLS 1.3 scenarios. However, they do not cover every possible configuration, extension, or edge case. An implementation that passes these vectors is not certified to be secure; it has only verified its key derivation and cryptographic operations against these specific examples.
sections.eli5: These answers are only for checking your math homework, not for keeping real secrets. Never use these test keys in a real secure connection.
